item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Kashmiris call India's rule settler-colonialism - and we should listen to them
item.description:
Kashmiris call India's rule settler-colonialism - and we should listen to them

Submitted by Sanaa Alimia on Fri, 06/26/2026 - 16:03
Such analysis reflects their lived realities, amid ongoing shifts in the region's land, law and demography
Indian paramilitary troopers stand deployed as Kashmiri Muslims take part in a ceremonial Ashura procession in Srinagar on 24 June 2026 (Tauseef Mustafa/AFP)
On

A rich body of journalism, creative writing and scholarship lays bare the violence of Indian military occupation and human rights abuses in Kashmir. It is quite a feat that Kashmiris themselves, facing state surveillance and the threat of detention and violence, are producing much of this work. 

Both within the country and in the diaspora, Kashmiris are seeking to write their own histories. By explaining the structures of power and their effects in Kashmir, they are producing some of the most precise analyses of the situation. 

They teach those of us who do not live under occupation not only what is happening, but why, including the historical forces and material conditions that sustain it.

Kashmiri voices are not just soundbites of suffering. They analyse, theorise and teach.

In recent years, both Kashmiri and non-Kashmiri thinkers have been unflinching in explaining India’s grip over Kashmir - not simply through tired debates around constitutional integration or the India-Pakistan territorial dispute, but through a rethinking of power and control. 

They ask a fundamental question: how should we understand the form of rule exercised over Kashmir?

For some, the answer lies in the framework of settler-colonialism. In Colonizing Kashmir, author Hafsa Kanjwal traces the long-term colonial logic of India’s occupation, while anthropologist Ather Zia’s scholarship documents the lived experiences of militarisation, disappearance and everyday governance under occupation, contributing to an emerging body of scholarship that interprets these dynamics through a colonial lens. 

In addition, journalist Azad Essa’s book Hostile Homelands situates Kashmir within a broader geopolitical framework, showing how deepening India-Israel ties are underpinned by shared Islamophobia, racialised ideologies, and alignment on ever-more explicit settler-colonial policies.

Transformations on the ground

These framings of India’s colonial logic in Kashmir are not simply theoretical. They emerge from documenting and understanding material conditions and transformations on the ground.

Kashmiri calls for liberation have deep roots. Collective memory recalls the tyranny of the Mughal Empire. But it was in the 1930s, under Hindu Dogra rule within the framework of British colonialism, that a modern mass movement for Kashmiri liberation began to take shape.

The partition of British India in 1947 reconfigured this struggle. Competing claims by India and Pakistan led to war, and in 1949, the United Nations brokered a ceasefire and established a de facto partition of Kashmir. India occupied the lion’s share of the Kashmir Valley, the heart of the struggle for Kashmiri self-determination, along with Jammu and Ladakh. Pakistan occupied smaller parts of the Kashmir Valley and Gilgit Baltistan. 

The analytical work being produced by Kashmiris is not peripheral. It is central to understanding emancipatory futures in South Asia and beyond

The UN called for a referendum to let people decide their future. It was never held. 

Shortly after the 1949 ceasefire, India granted Jammu and Kashmir a form of autonomy under Article 370, allowing for its own constitution, flag and residency protections. But key domains - defence, foreign affairs, finance and communications - remained under Delhi’s control, and reliant on local collaborating elites.

The facade of autonomy could not conceal a deeper reality: Kashmiris did not want symbolic autonomy in return for material inclusion within India. They wanted freedom.

These demands would explode in 1989 and continue through the 1990s in the form of a mass uprising. Dubbed the “Kashmiri intifada” in international media, having broken out at around the same time as the first Palestinian intifada, Kashmiri demands for freedom have persisted ever since. 

While resistance has taken on an armed dimension, often with the interference of the Pakistani state, these demands for liberation remain rooted in popular will, which has an agency of its own.

Since the 1990s, Indian state forces have tortured, disappeared and killed tens of thousands of Kashmiris.  Dreams have been torn asunder, with families split across borders and exiled. The Armed Forces (Special Powers) Act grants India sweeping control, including the use of lethal force - and it has been widely deployed.

Rapid reconfiguration 

It is within this longer history that recent developments must be understood.

In 2019, the right-wing government of Prime Minister Narendra Modi revoked Article 370, and reorganised the region into two union territories: Jammu and Kashmir in the west, and Ladakh in the east. This marked a decisive shift in the legal and political structure of rule. 

Journalists and scholars - as well as the Kashmiri people themselves - interpreted this moment not as a beginning, but as an intensification: a move towards a more formalised and explicit settler-colonial project.

The significance of 2019 lies in how it has rapidly reconfigured the relationships among land, sovereignty and population. Article 370 restricted land ownership and residency to Kashmiris; its removal has opened the doors to Indian settlement, which is being taken up at speed. 

Legal changes now enable land acquisition, evictions and property confiscations from Kashmiris. These policies are designed to alter the facts on the ground by reshaping the demographic balances in the territories.

These transformations have unfolded alongside intensified repression: the detention of journalists, communications blackouts, passport confiscations, digital surveillance, and restrictions on movement. Together, these measures point to a restructuring of rule that is not adequately captured by older frameworks of integration, autonomy or even occupation.

Yet the language of settler-colonialism remains largely ignored, often dismissed in ham-fisted ways without serious engagement.

Voices marginalised

In May 2025, for example, a brief armed conflict broke out between India and Pakistan after an attack in Kashmir killed two dozen Indian tourists. India conducted air strikes in Pakistan, claiming it was targeting “terrorist infrastructure”, and Pakistan retaliated. Nationalistic fervour in India and Pakistan reached a peak. 

Once again, Kashmiris were sidelined - reduced to instruments within competing national narratives, if they were mentioned at all. Their voices were marginalised not only in India and Pakistan, but across international media, even as they faced the brunt of the violence.

Even among segments of the South Asian left, the reluctance to centre Kashmiri voices and take seriously their analysis is, as Essa details, indicative of the political limits of solidarity, with the “Kashmir issue” constrained by inherited commitments to postcolonial state sovereignty.

How India is implementing the 'Israel model' in Kashmir
Read More »

Such approaches fail to confront how postcolonial states themselves can exercise forms of domination - through internal colonisation, sub-imperial regional power, or, in some cases, settler-colonial practices. 

Formal independence did not produce emancipation for all. Instead, hierarchies of class, caste and religion, alongside regimes of legal exception and incomplete projects of self-determination, have structured differentiated forms of citizenship and belonging.

In this context, the analytical work being produced by Kashmiris is not peripheral. It is central to understanding emancipatory futures in South Asia and beyond.

Listening, in this sense, is not an ethical gesture, but a political one. To engage seriously with Kashmir, and to be a genuine ally, means recognising Kashmiris not as objects of empathy, but as producers of knowledge about their own condition. 

Sidelining their analysis reproduces the very structures of domination that many analysts seek to critique, and this needs to be acknowledged. Only then can meaningful solidarity emerge. 

The views expressed in this article belong to the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Middle East Eye.

Dozens of settlers erected a tent and brought water tanks and storage containers to Tel al-Asur, between the towns of al-Mughayyir and Deir Jarir, east of Ramallah, local sources told Wafa.

The sources said the area had faced escalating violent settler attacks, land seizures and settlement expansion.

Settlers also established outposts on land belonging to Deir Istiya, north of Salfit, and Umm Safa, northwest of Ramallah, earlier on Sunday.

Settlers established 42 outposts on Palestinian-owned land in the first half of 2026, most of them pastoral, according to the Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission. These included 13 in Hebron governorate, nine in Ramallah, eight in Nablus and four in Bethlehem.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Tunisia: Ghannouchi’s daughter says family denied information after his collapse in prison
item.description:
Tunisia: Ghannouchi’s daughter says family denied information after his collapse in prison

Submitted by Bilge Kotan on Sun, 07/26/2026 - 21:17
The jailed opposition leader was reportedly taken to hospital after fainting more than a week ago in Mornaguia Prison amid temperatures above 50 degrees Celsius
In this file photo, Rached Ghannouchi, former head of the Ennahdha party, answers questions during an interview with AFP at his office in Tunis on 31 March 2022 (AFP)
Off

The daughter of jailed Tunisian Ennahda leader Rached Ghannouchi said his family had been denied all contact with him and information about his condition for more than a week after the 84-year-old reportedly fainted amid high temperatures and was taken to hospital.

Concerns have emerged over the opposition leader’s health after an eyewitness said she saw him lose consciousness inside Mornaguia Prison.

“Where is my father? Where are they hiding him? Why prevent visits?” Soumaya Ghannouchi said in a video posted on Instagram.

She said lawyers seeking to visit him at the prison were told he had been transferred to hospital. But when a lawyer and her mother went to the hospital, authorities refused them entry or any information, she added.

“The last thing we heard from the lawyers was that my father felt dizzy and fainted during the visit due to heat exhaustion,” she said, adding that temperatures inside the prison had exceeded 50 degrees Celsius.

Ghannouchi said her father had Parkinson’s disease and a thyroid disorder requiring specialised care and described his detention in a cell without cooling as a threat to his life, accusing the justice system of pursuing "revenge".

"Wasn't it enough to sentence him to over 150 years in prison on fabricated, absurd charges that no rational mind would believe, along with a life sentence and 10 years of administrative probation?" she said.

Ghannouchi, a former parliament speaker and leader of the Ennahda movement, has been jailed since April 2023 amid an intensified crackdown on political opponents by President Kais Saied’s government.

The leader's imprisonment has come to symbolise the broader campaign against opposition figures that followed Saied’s suspension of parliament, dismissal of the government and move to rule by decree in July 2021. Critics described those measures as a coup against Tunisia’s democratic transition.

The leader's daughter demanded access to his medical file and information about his treatment and medication, calling this a basic right of a prisoner, his family and his lawyers.

Ghannouchi also said Tunisian President Kais Saied and Justice Minister Leila Jaffel were “morally, politically and legally responsible” for any harm suffered by her father.

Qatari Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani spoke by phone with Omani Foreign Minister Sayyid Badr Albusaidi, discussing bilateral ties and joint coordination to de-escalate tensions in the Middle East, Al Jazeera reported.

Qatar fully supports the efforts to defuse tensions and reach a comprehensive agreement for sustainable peace in the region, Qatari prime minister said.

item.title: [www.middleeasteye.net] Tunisia: Ghannouchi’s daughter says family denied information after his collapse in prison
item.description:
Tunisia: Ghannouchi’s daughter says family denied information after his collapse in prison

The daughter of jailed Tunisian Ennahda leader Rached Ghannouchi said his family had been denied all contact with him and information about his condition for more than a week after the 84-year-old reportedly fainted amid high temperatures and was taken to hospital.

Concerns have emerged over the opposition leader’s health after an eyewitness said she saw him lose consciousness inside Mornaguia Prison.

“Where is my father? Where are they hiding him? Why prevent visits?” Soumaya Ghannouchi said in a video posted on Instagram.

She said lawyers seeking to visit him at the prison were told he had been transferred to hospital. But when a lawyer and her mother went to the hospital, authorities refused them entry or any information, she added.

“The last thing we heard from the lawyers was that my father felt dizzy and fainted during the visit due to heat exhaustion,” she said, adding that temperatures inside the prison had exceeded 50 degrees Celsius.

Read more: Ghannouchi’s daughter says family denied information after his collapse in prison

item.description:

Reform UK’s plan to make employers pay an annual levy for overseas staff would harm the NHS and social care, cause a shortage of schoolteachers, and could push some universities into bankruptcy, experts have warned.

Nigel Farage’s party has pledged a “migrant worker surcharge”, which would involve a higher rate of employer national insurance as well as a separate annual charge. It would apply to any employees without a UK passport, including EU nationals with settled status, with the exception of Irish passport holders.

item.description:
Morning update

Good morning Middle East Eye readers,

Here are the latest developments: 

  • The Iranian foreign ministry spokesman said that they are continuing to exchange message with the US, but accused Washington of undermining diplomacy efforts. Esmaeil Baqaei told Austria’s ORF television the US destroyed and violated conditions that are vital for negotiations.

  • US President Donald Trump on Sunday shared a series of AI-generated images on his social media platform Truth Social, depicting the seizure of an Iranian oil tanker and a strike on Iran's Kharg oil export terminal.

  • Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said on Sunday a Ukrainian attack on an Iranian commercial vessel "cannot go unanswered". He said on X that this was "a blatant UN Charter violation done at Israel's behest to drag Europe into its war".

  • Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa said in an interview with Al Jazeera that a successful security deal with Israel could pave the way for comprehensive peace without compromising Syria’s right to the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights. 

  • Israel's security cabinet has approved allowing a proposed international force for Gaza to enter parts of the enclave that are not under Israeli occupation, according to an Israeli official. The proposed International Security Force is part of the US-backed plan for Gaza proposed in October.

  • Israeli settlers established three new outposts on Palestinian-owned land in the occupied West Bank on Sunday, the Wafa news agency reported. Dozens of settlers erected in Tel al-Asur, between the towns of al-Mughayyir and Deir Jarir, east of Ramallah.

item.title: [World news | The Guardian] Monday briefing: ​How the Cockroach ​protests ​have expose​d the ​cracks in ​India’s government
item.description:
In today’s newsletter: Across ​the country, a ​younger generation is turning private disillusionment into public defiance​ against a government that once felt untouchable

Good morning. As flames engulfed parts of France and Spain this weekend, in India, the prime minister, Narendra Modi, was trying to put out a very different kind of fire. Thousands of people arrived in Delhi on Saturday to demand the resignation of his education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan. When he stepped down in the early afternoon, the protests turned into a triumphant block party.

But the Cockroach protests that have swept through India this summer are about much more than a single minister. They have humiliated Modi and undermined the indomitable power of his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) that has ruled India for the past 12 years. They’re also a lesson in using humour to political advantage.

Wild fires | Authorities in France battled to contain a huge wildfire near Bordeaux in the south-west as Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, warned Spain and the Iberian peninsula were suffering the effects of the climate emergency.

Germany | A man suspected of driving a van into a crowd near Berlin’s Pride festival then going on a knife rampage in an Islamist terror attack has been shot dead by police, German officials have said.

Iran | The US has paused strikes on Iran for a second night as top military officials advised Donald Trump to halt his bombing campaign, and diplomatic negotiations have continued to avoid a return to all-out war.

UK politics | Britain’s foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, is to indicate he will put the climate crisis and overseas development at the heart of UK international relations by taking up the country’s seat on the board at the World Bank.

UK news | Five Palestine Action activists face being sentenced as terrorists for breaking windows and throwing red paint at a branch of Barclays Bank in Lancashire.

Monday | Andrew and Tristan Tate are due back in the Florida court where they’re fighting their extradition to the UK, to face rape and sex-trafficking charges.

Tuesday | Donald Trump and Volodymyr Zelenskyy are expected to be among those attending the Washington DC memorial service for the late South Carolina senator and Trump ally Lindsey Graham.

Thursday | People will go to the polls to elect the next mayor of Greater Manchester, who will replace Andy Burnham.
